Hi Alice — thanks for the heads-up and for the headers/screenshot. Sorry you're hitting this. A few quick things while we triage: 

1) Quick troubleshooting steps for you to try (low effort, often helps):
   - Try the invite link in a private/incognito window (clears cookies/session bindings).
   - If possible, try a different browser (Chrome vs Safari) or clear site cookies for coupa.com.
   - If you're on a corporate network, try a personal hotspot in case a proxy is rewriting headers.

2) What I already did on my side:
   - Escalated to our infra/portal team and opened CASE-7921 (internal).
   - Attached your headers to the ticket.

3) Temporary workaround: I can revoke the current invite and issue a fresh invite with an extended TTL and a different binding strategy. That usually resolves token drift issues for vendors that use strict cookie partitioning.

Could you confirm: browser + version, OS, and whether the vendor admin is trying to accept behind a VPN/proxy? If you'd like me to send a fresh invite now, I can — just say the word and I'll include Ben to regenerate the token.

I'll keep you posted.

—Chloë

From: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.com>

Date: 2029-06-11T08:23:00-07:00
Subject: INTERNAL: Investigation notes — sentinel invite token binding

Chloë / Monica — quick summary of what I found after looking at the headers Alice attached:

- Observed server-side: Accept endpoint logs show a rejected request with error code "TOKEN_BIND_MISMATCH". The incoming request has an Accept cookie that does not match the invite's binding cookie (X-Invite-Bind).
- Probable cause: Vendor devices appear to be sending an older session cookie (cookie re-use across subdomains) that doesn't align with our current sameSite/samePath token binding. We also saw that the invite token TTL was set to 8 hours (default); if their system attempted acceptance after session rotation we hit the mismatch.

Action plan (short):
1) Revoke and reissue invite with extended TTL (48 hrs) and generate a new token without the strict samePath attribute. That's quick and low risk.
2) Add a transient fallback on the accept endpoint to allow token rebind if certain headers match (requires a small runtime patch; target for next deploy if we see more cases).
3) Notify the customer with a fresh link and ask them to try incognito first.

I can run (1) now if Chloë authorizes. I linked the internal case: https://redwood.example.com/internal/cases/CASE-7921 (logs + header dump).

-ben
